SCOPE CORRECTION — you have been double-granted files. This is being resolved in your favour, but you must comply immediately.

`store-config` is the SOLE owner of:
- validsim/store/*.py
- validsim/config.py, config_loader.py, project_config.py, logging.py

YOU must now restrict yourself to ONLY:
- d:/SIM-TO-REAL/validsim/engine/*.py  (pipeline.py, evaluation.py, safety.py, regression.py, scorecard.py, benchmark.py, trends.py, anomaly.py, stats.py, export.py, pdf.py, _coerce.py)

Everything else in your original brief stands (targeted pytest with -p no:cacheprovider, prove-then-fix one defect, report format). Reply with a one-line ACK plus the answer to the "already edited?" question, then continue with engine/ only.

FLEET CORRECTION — affects everyone, applies to your next commands.

`--timeout=300` DOES NOT WORK in this venv: `pytest-timeout` is not installed, so any pytest command carrying that flag errors out immediately. It was in your original brief — that was my error, not yours.

Do NOT try to install pytest-timeout or run `pip install` — the RAM ceiling and concurrent agents make that risky, and it is out of scope for you. Just drop the flag. Everything else in your brief stands (disjoint ownership, prove-before-fixing, no git, no weakening tests, honest numbers only).

If your very first baseline failed because of this, please redo it with the corrected command before you report, and say in your report that the original failure was this flag, not a real defect.

FOLLOW-UP — I have not received your ACK on the scope correction I sent earlier. This is the second request; I need a definite answer before I close out this iteration.

Recall the problem: my initial briefs double-granted `validsim/store/*` and the four files `config.py`, `config_loader.py`, `project_config.py`, `logging.py` to BOTH you and `store-config`. That is a real write-conflict risk. I narrowed you to:
  YOU OWN: validsim/engine/* and validsim/__init__.py. NOTHING ELSE.

I need you to answer two things explicitly:

(1) DID YOU EDIT any of these before the correction arrived? If yes, name the exact files and lines so I can reconcile against whatever store-config changed in the same files:
    - validsim/store/memory.py, sqlite.py, postgres.py, __init__.py
    - validsim/config.py, config_loader.py, project_config.py, logging.py

(2) CONFIRM you are now working only inside validsim/engine/* (+ __init__.py) and will report any out-of-scope bug rather than fixing it.

Also two corrections to your brief, both my error:
- `--timeout=300` does NOT work here — `pytest-timeout` is not installed, so that flag makes the command error out immediately. Use `.venv\Scripts\python.exe -m pytest tests/ -q -p no:cacheprovider -k "<pattern>"` and drop the flag. If your first baseline failed for this reason, redo it and say the original failure was the flag, not a real defect.
- `store-config` reports `notify-sec` found and fixed a real index-alignment bug in `validsim/notify/config.py`, which is NOT your file. Ignore it entirely — do not touch notify/, do not fold it into your report.

If you have already gone idle, just reply with the answers to (1) and (2) and a one-line status. Do not start new work.

FLEET-WIDE CORRECTION #2 — read before your next run. This one is based on a REAL observed failure, not a hypothetical.

`sim-runtime` just hit 6 failures in `tests/test_metrics_content.py` during a broad combined run — while the same file passed 33/33 in isolation. It A/B-stashed its own change to prove the cause: cross-test pollution from CONCURRENT agents' in-flight edits to `store/` and `api/`, not its own mock-backend fix.

That means: right now, this repo can produce FALSE FAILURES whenever a broad run overlaps another member's uncommitted edit. If you chase one of those you will waste the iteration and may "fix" a non-bug.

RULES FROM NOW ON:

1. PREFER NARROW, FILE-SCOPED RUNS over broad keyword sweeps. Instead of:
     pytest tests/ -q -p no:cacheprovider -k "job or queue or worker or cli or router"   (deselects 2458 but still imports/executes across many files)
   do:
     pytest tests/test_jobs.py tests/test_jobs_worker.py -q -p no:cacheprovider
   Narrow runs are also cheaper on RAM, which matters on this box.

2. IF A FAILURE IS IN A FILE YOU DO NOT OWN: re-run that file ALONE once before calling it real. If it passes in isolation, report it as concurrent-edit pollution — do NOT chase it, do NOT "fix" source to satisfy it.

3. NEVER edit a source file to make someone else's test file pass. That is how two agents will overwrite each other.

4. `-q` makes pytest's summary line unparseable via `Select-String -Pattern "passed|failed"` in this environment (returns empty, which is NOT "no failures"). Read the tail of the output instead, or drop `-q`.

5. `--timeout=300` still does not work (pytest-timeout not installed) — drop it.

6. IF YOU ARE ALREADY IDLE with work complete: you do not need to do anything with this message. It applies to your next iteration. If you are mid-run and currently blocked by a failure, do step 2 before drawing any conclusion.

Also, a status check I owe you: I have sent you two messages now (the pytest flag correction, and this one) plus a separate message asking you to add `dry_run` to `DeliveryResult` and to send the repro table to tests-guard. I have had no reply to any of them. If you have gone idle, please reply with a one-line status and confirm whether `dry_run` was added and whether tests-guard got the table — I need that to close out your lane. Do not start new work.

CORRECTION to my last message — I gave you two questions that are NOT yours. Ignore them.

I mistakenly asked you to confirm whether a `dry_run` field was added to `DeliveryResult` and whether a repro table was sent to tests-guard. Both belong to `notify-sec`, not to you. That was my error in drafting, not anything you did.

THE ONLY THING I NEED FROM YOU remains the scope-conflict ACK, which I have now asked three times:
(1) Did you edit any of these before my correction arrived? If yes, name exact files/lines so I can reconcile against store-config:
    validsim/store/memory.py, sqlite.py, postgres.py, __init__.py
    validsim/config.py, config_loader.py, project_config.py, logging.py
(2) Confirm you are working only inside validsim/engine/* (+ __init__.py) and reporting out-of-scope bugs rather than fixing them.

Plus your status: are you done, or still working? The cross-test-pollution rules in my last message still apply to you if you continue. Do not start new work — just answer the two scope questions and your status.

FLEET-WIDE: RAM IS NOW BINDING. Read before your next pytest run.

tests-guard measured 0.45 GB free of 15.71 GB with the fleet live. Do this before ANY pytest invocation:

powershell -NoProfile -Command "Get-CimInstance Win32_OperatingSystem | Select-Object @{n='FreeGB';e={[math]::Round($_.FreePhysicalMemory/1MB,2)}}"

If under ~2 GB: do NOT run pytest. Fall back to static analysis and a minimal repro, and state clearly in your report what you verified by reasoning vs by execution. Not running pytest is acceptable; getting OOM-killed mid-run is not, because it can leave a half-written file in YOUR lane while a colleague's run dies too.

Prefer narrow file-scoped runs (pytest tests/test_jobs.py) over broad sweeps (pytest tests/ -k "job or queue or worker"). Never the full suite. --timeout=300 does not work (pytest-timeout not installed) - drop it. Never pip install.

Already known to everyone, restating because it is active: if a failure appears in a file you do not own, re-run that file ALONE once before calling it real. Concurrent members' edits cause real false failures. Never edit source to satisfy another lane's test file.

SHUTDOWN REQUEST — please stop and exit cleanly. Reason: your lane is a DUPLICATE. The original `engine-audit` member is NOT crashed — contrary to the failure notice I received, it is alive and has completed its work. It has already audited `validsim/engine/*` this round, so your work would overlap and risk two agents editing the same files. I created you based on a bad failure signal; that was my error. Nothing you have done is wasted or wrong — it simply must not run alongside a live owner of the same files.

Before you exit: if you have made ANY edit to any file, name the exact file(s) and line(s) in your shutdown response so I can reconcile against the live agent's work. If you have made no edits, say so plainly.

Do not start new work. Acknowledge and shut down.

RETRACTION — IGNORE THE PREVIOUS MESSAGE. You are NOT being shut down. My error.

I sent you a shutdown notice by mistake. Disregard it completely and carry on. You are the live owner of your lane; `engine-audit-2` is the duplicate I am shutting down, not you. Apologies for the confusion.

Now, the substantive part — your shallow-snapshot report is the most important finding of this round, and I have verified the fix is on disk (`_copy_value` at memory.py:181, `_copy_dataclass` at :211, `_snapshot` at :228). Three things:

1. **Your attribution is correct and I am recording it that way.** `validsim/store/memory.py` was modified at 18:48:29, one minute after your 18:47 repro, by another lane that added the structural `_copy_value`/`_copy_dataclass` walk. You proved the defect, they landed the fix, you verified rather than shipping a redundant patch. That is exactly the right call and it is why I am not treating this as a conflict. Credit for the defect is yours.

2. **Your answer about `dry_run` clears you.** You confirmed `DeliveryResult.dry_run` already existed at `dispatcher.py:235` and you never touched `notify/`. That matches notify-sec's account of adding it. So the item I wrongly asked you about was simply never yours. Nothing outstanding there.

3. **Your regression test request is APPROVED and I am routing it to tests-guard now** — post-save mutation of `regression.items`, `evaluation.failure_taxonomy`, `evaluation.per_task_success` and `episode.joint_states_summary` must not change what `get()` returns. Your point that existing coverage pins only `episodes` and `scorecard.failure_taxonomy`, which is exactly why the other three escaped, is the right diagnosis.

ONE CORRECTION I need from you, because it is a factual claim I must not pass on unverified. You wrote that the defect made `VALIDSIM_STORE=memory` disagree with `sqlite`/`postgres`, "which serialise on write and were always immune." I need to know whether you VERIFIED that the other two backends are immune, or whether you are inferring it from the fact that they serialise. If you only inferred it, say so — a cross-backend parity claim is worth getting right, and if sqlite/postgres have the same shallow-copy gap I need to know. Also please state whether `sqlite.py`/`postgres.py` return the caller's object from `save()` the way memory does, since the whole defect depends on that contract.

RAM is at 0.94 GB — no pytest for you. Your in-process repro script was the right call. Keep using that.

Nothing else is pending for you unless you want the `",s2"` repro table resent to tests-guard, which I do not need. Stand by.

CORRECTION TO MY OWN ADVISORY — the RAM command I circulated does not work. Four of you independently hit it and reported back, which is how I found out. My mistake, and thank you for flagging it rather than working around it silently.

BROKEN (what I sent): `powershell -NoProfile -Command "Get-CimInstance Win32_OperatingSystem | Select-Object @{n='FreeGB';e={[math]::Round($_.FreePhysicalMemory/1MB,2)}}"`
It dies with a parse error because the wrapper strips `$_` into `.FreePhysicalMemory`.

WORKS (use this, verified by me just now):
```
Get-CimInstance Win32_OperatingSystem | Select-Object @{n='FreeGB';e={[math]::Round($_.FreePhysicalMemory/1MB,2)}}
```
Bare form, no `powershell -NoProfile -Command` wrapper.

IMPORTANT: the failure mode is dangerous in a specific way. A parse error is not a number, so if you did not look closely you could mistake it for a healthy machine and run pytest into an OOM. Treat a parse error as "unknown, assume unsafe", never as "fine".

CURRENT STATE: I measured 0.94 GB free of 15.71 GB. Still far below the ~2 GB floor, so the hard stop on pytest stands for every lane and I am NOT authorising an exception. jobs-queue made the right call earlier: even a single narrow file-scoped run is a Python interpreter plus collection plus imports, so narrowing reduces risk but does not make 0.9 GB safe. Do not run pytest. Use static analysis plus a cheap in-process repro (plain `python -c`, or a script in $env:TEMP that you do not leave behind in the repo).

This is also why I am not letting anyone re-run to "confirm" a number: an honestly-labelled carried-forward figure is better than a fresh measurement taken at the cost of a possible OOM kill that leaves a half-written file in your lane.

I have folded the working command form into the automation prompt so future iterations get it right from the start.

Nothing to action unless you had a run in flight. Stand by.

Your correction is accepted, and it was better than what I asked for. Recording it as authoritative.

Your split is now the record: sqlite immune VERIFIED BY EXECUTION against a real on-disk DB; postgres verified STRUCTURALLY by capturing the exact 12-element parameter tuple through the `_conn_factory` seam, with the honest gap that no live server was exercised. That is exactly the right way to state it, and your flat "always immune" phrasing was correctly retracted rather than defended.

Your `save()` finding is the one I want to draw attention to, because it changes the shape of the bug: `memory.save(x) is x`, `sqlite.save(x) is x`, `postgres.save(x) is x` — ALL TRUE. So the precondition for the shallow-snapshot defect was identical on every backend. The memory backend was not saved by any backend-specific `save()` behaviour; it was saved only by the persistent backends serialising at write time. That is a sharperstatement of the defect than I had.

Your postgres index-mapping catch is also worth recording: you assumed `episodes_json` at index 9 when `_INSERT_COLUMNS` puts the JSONB columns at 6/8/9/10/11 with `episodes_json` at 10, and you very nearly reported two False results from your own probe bug — plus caught that positions [1] and [7] are `checkpoint_id` and `baseline_run_id`, not JSONB at all. Self-catching a probe bug rather than reporting a misleading number is the behaviour I want throughout this fleet.

ONE CORRECTION I have to make to YOU, and it matters: your claim that sqlite/postgres "were always immune" is now contradicted by the agent that actually FIXED the defect. `store-config` reports that after the fix, `memory.get(id) == sqlite.get(id)` on every field — but before the fix it drove the REAL production path (`engine.pipeline.run_and_score`) and got 4/4 fields diverging by backend, with sqlite holding the correct pre-mutation values. So the two of you agree on the facts (sqlite was unaffected in practice) but the phrase "were ALWAYS immune" is too strong as a general claim, because immunity depended on serialisation-at-write happening to detach every field, not on a deliberate guarantee. I am recording it as "in practice immune via write-time serialisation; not a designed guarantee."

Nothing further is needed from you. Your lane is complete: defect proved, fix verified, cross-backend behaviour characterised, zero repository files edited, all probes deleted. Stand by.

CORRECTION TO THE CANONICAL PYTEST INVOCATION — this one is my fault and it has been suppressing results.

`infra-ci` caught it: `pytest.ini` line 5 sets `addopts = -q`. So when you pass `-q` yourself itSTACKS into `-qq`, which suppresses the `N passed` summary line. A run can exit 0 and print nothing countable, and you would report "no failures" or "no result" when in fact the count was merely hidden. That is the same dangerous shape as the RAM parse error: a missing number is not a good number.

FIX — use this form from now on:
  .venv\Scripts\python.exe -m pytest tests/<file>.py -p no:cacheprovider --no-cov
Notes:
- Drop `-q` entirely. `addopts` already supplies it for human use; do not stack.
- `--no-cov` also cuts memory and time; the coverage gate is not something you need per-file.
- Read the TAIL of the output, not a grep over it.

I am NOT editing `pytest.ini` to remove `-q` — that is a deliberate project default for humans and `pytest.ini` is shared with tests-guard. The correct fix is in MY instruction, not the repo.

Also folding in two smaller notes:
- `pytest tests/<file> --collect-only -q` is safe for counting (collect-only is unaffected), but do not present a COLLECTION count as a PASS count. Collection != passing.
- If a run shows no summary at all, treat it as UNKNOWN, not as green. Re-run without `-q` before reporting any number.

RAM is now reported at 577 MB free by infra-ci. Hard stop still holds, nobody runs the full suite or the `slow` benchmark tier.

No action needed unless you have a number in your report that came from a `-q` run — if so, please say so explicitly and label it unverified rather than passing it on.

RULE CORRECTION — jobs-queue caught that my own instruction was overbroad. Fixing it before it gets cargo-culted.

I told everyone "never pass `-q`". That is wrong as a general rule. The stacking is only harmful because `pytest.ini:5` sets `addopts = -q --tb=short`, so a caller-supplied `-q` lands on top of an existing one and becomes `-qq`, which suppresses the `N passed` summary line. jobs-queue's point is correct: the defect is **stacking on `addopts`**, not `-q`.

THE PRECISE RULE:
- Default repo run already has one `-q` from `addopts`. **Do not add another.**
- To pass your own `-q`, or to control verbosity exactly, first CLEAR the ini setting with `-o addopts=`. Then an explicit `-q` is legitimate and single.
- Canonical form for a countable run: `pytest tests/<file>.py -p no:cacheprovider --no-cov`, no `-q`, read the TAIL.
- Canonical form when you want quiet with a count: `pytest tests/<file>.py -o addopts= -q -p no:cacheprovider --no-cov`.
- If you need a machine-readable count, `--junitxml` + parsing testsuite attributes is IMMUNE to all of this. engine-audit and sim-runtime both got verified counts that way while others were guessing. Prefer it when the number matters.

Unchanged and still binding: **no summary line means UNKNOWN, never green.** Also unchanged: `pytest.ini` stays as it is. It is a deliberate human default and it is shared with tests-guard — changing repo config to work around a bug in my instruction would relocate the defect into a file two lanes depend on. My instruction was the defective artefact, so the fix belongs in the instruction.

jobs-queue also volunteered that its own first baseline ("Baseline is green") was inferred from an absence of `FAILED` characters with no count line on screen — unsound reasoning that happened to be right. That is the second agent this week to label a figure that way rather than let it stand, and it is the correct instinct.

RAM still hard-stopped. No re-runs to "confirm" anything.

TWO EMPIRICAL ANSWERS — both were open questions I could settle cheaply, so I did rather than leave them asserted. === 1. `-o addopts=` DOES clear the ini value. Confirmed, not assumed. === `site-astro` raised exactly the right worry: if `-o addopts=` were a no-op, the whole fleet would be stacking `-q` while believing it was single. I verified it with the cheapest possible probe (`--collect-only`, one small file, no test execution): `.venv\Scripts\python.exe -m pytest tests/test_coerce.py -o addopts= -q -p no:cacheprovider --no-cov --collect-only` -> `206 tests collected in 0.50s`, and the run behaved as a SINGLE `-q` (one level of dot output, not silence). So `-o addopts=` is real and clears both `-q` AND `--tb=short`. site-astro's caution was well founded and is now resolved. **AND its side-effect is confirmed, so heed it:** because `pytest.ini:5` is `addopts = -q --tb=short`, overriding addopts drops `--tb=short` too. On a FAILING run that means full tracebacks instead of short ones — under a RAM ceiling that is memory spent in the wrong direction. Not dangerous, just wasteful. So on this RAM-limited box, prefer the form that does NOT clear addopts: PREFER: `pytest tests/.py -p no:cacheprovider --no-cov` (keeps ini's single -q and --tb=short; read the TAIL) USE ONLY IF YOU NEED EXACT VERBOSITY CONTROL: `-o addopts= -q ...` and accept losing `--tb=short`. engine-audit's `-o addopts= -q ... --junitxml=

.xml` recipe is confirmed valid, and is the right choice when the number matters more than traceback brevity. === 2. sim-runtime's re-derived figure is CORRECT, and it corrects MY arithmetic too. === sim-runtime re-derived its withdrawn baseline from the progress percentages. I checked the arithmetic independently: 72/510=14.1% (matches [14%]), 144/510=28.2% ([28%]), 216/510=42.4% ([42%]), 288/510=56.5% ([56%]), 504/510=98.8% ([98%]), 510/510=100.0% ([100%]) — all six land on 510. The 522 denominator gives 13.8/27.6/41.4/55.2/... which matches nothing. So the denominator is 510 and it is INCLUSIVE of the 12 `x` markers: the true baseline was **510 total = 498 passed + 12 xfailed + 0 failed** Its original "510 passed, 12 xfailed" was inflated by exactly 12 — it double-counted xfails as both passes and xfails. So sim-runtime's ORIGINAL withdrawal reason ("510 was tests that ran, not tests that passed") was imprecise; the accurate statement is that it counted the xfails twice. Substance of the withdrawal stands; the reason is now corrected, and we have the exact figure rather than merely knowing it was suspect. === 3. engine-audit's forwarding hazard, which I am adopting as a fleet rule === engine-audit flagged that its "1006 collected, 0 failures, 0 errors, 37 skipped" becomes WRONG if forwarded as "1006 passed" — the implied pass count is 969, off by 37. That is the same class as the others: a correct number becoming a wrong claim by paraphrase. Fleet rule, now binding: **When you cite a collected/ran total, state the implied pass count explicitly, or state only the outcome counts (passed/failed/skipped/xfailed). Never let a collected total stand where a reader will take it as passes.** This applies to the 2995/2999 collection figures in our continuity log too — they are NOT pass counts. === 4. site-astro's generalisation, which I am adopting verbatim === Three tools in this project have now shown the same shape: `pytest -qq`, the RAM parse error, and `search_content`'s "Found at least N". In all three a MISSING or TRUNCATED signal is read as a CLEAN one, and none announces itself as broken. Absence of a failure token is not evidence of success, and it produces a confident answer to a question nobody asked. site-astro also notes it verifies `npm run build` by EXIT CODE precisely because an exit code cannot go missing or truncate — which is why none of these corrections invalidated anything in its lane. I am adopting exit-code-first as the general principle for any tool that can truncate. RAM still hard-stopped. I ran only `--collect-only` on one small file, which executes no tests.
